newsitem.title: CHINA: FUND VIEW-Funds stay away as Asia currencies waver.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Funds stay away as Asia currencies waver.

text.p: Fund flows in Asian markets are expected to remain scarce this week with institutional investors sticking firmly to the sidelines in the wake of volatility in regional currency markets.
"It's all very speculative. There are not a lot of funds," one head trader at a major brokerage said.
Traders said fund flows have dried up with stock markets straggling along in the wake of roiled currencies. Little change is forecast in the next few trading sessions as currencies seek direction.

A vicious bout of volatility on Friday was compounded by apparent inaction by the region's central banks, which usually intervene aggressively to keep currencies on an even keel and pegged to the U.S. dollar, or a basket of currencies heavily weighted in the U.S. dollar.
The Thai baht continued to ease, prompting speculation about the Malaysian ringgit, which hit a three-year low against the U.S. dollar with the central bank apparently inactive.
The Singapore dollar, whose graph against the U.S. dollar is often described as "a dead man's heartbeat," initially followed suit, hitting a 30-month low.
The move was described as a competitive devaluation with the ringgit, but the Singapore dollar later recovered on unconfirmed speculation that the central bank might intervene soon.
The Philippines peso moved violently and then seemed to stabilise, while the Indonesian rupiah slid to a new low.
Currency forward markets were active and volatile.

Traders reported institutional interest in the Philippines stock market, which soared 52 points on Friday after central bank Governor Gabriel Singson said he would tap the country's US$1.05 billion International Monetary Fund aid package.
"Where it goes from here, God knows," one Hong Kong trader said. Local traders were expecting a test of resistance at 2,700 after the main index closed at 2,672 on Friday.
Buying of Thai stocks was minimal, although some interest was reported at its weakest levels. Thailand's main index ended Friday's session 2.91 points weaker at 653.37.

And in Malaysia, the market broke the 1,000 mark. "There are sell programs around but they (fund managers) don't think the currency will devalue. If it does, the equity market will follow the same pattern," the Hong Kong trader said. Kuala Lumpur's main index closed 2.4 points easier at 1,001.55 on Friday.
One fund manager, who asked not to be identified, said: "A consensus is forming that the Thai baht has further to go, the peso is stabilising and the rupiah is just about right."
Further weakness was forecast in the Malaysian ringgit, but any depreciation would fail to match the fall in the Thai baht because Malaysia's economy was relatively healthy.
"So I think the focus for most people is how bad can it get in Thailand, how far down will it go in Malaysia, and did we overreact in the Philippines," the fund manager said.
Hong Kong and Bombay stand out as safe havens, although most strategists seem to be adopting a cautious view before committing themselves to a firm switch in asset allocations.
"Until regional capital markets settle down, we remain heavily committed to the Indian story, a market which seems to be benefiting from all this volatility," Merrill Lynch said.
Hong Kong also managed to attract institutional funds last week, with buying dominated by Hongkong Bank, which traders said gained as a virtual proxy for Hang Seng index futures.
